男女之理皆於此乎形見幽隱者自爾而昭灼
矣不有以著萬物之理乎夫樂之爲用能奮德
punctuated: 豈無成功之可言乎？彼人心之德，藏於寂，初未有光之可見也。惟樂爲能奮之，詠間克諧，而和順之積中者，自不秘其英華之發；行列交綴，而美善之根心者，自莫巳其暢達之機。情之深者，文之明，而輝光之發越，固將過之而愈楊矣。何者？德寓於樂之中，故樂作而光奮，勢之所必至也。四時之氣，運於天，若難必其皆和也。惟樂爲能動之，越之聲容，則以和敦和，而春夏之仁動，不至於散也；施之金石，則以順助順，而秋冬之義靜，不至於密也。感之深者，化之神，而眞機之保合，固將循軌而莫違矣。何者？樂由天而作，故樂行而和動，機之不容間也。至於萬物之理，至賾不可紀也，樂又能以著之。蓋其聲氣之充實，通乎倫理，故節奏之合，自然於形容。以比終始之序，則君臣民事物之理，悉於此乎呈象，渾然者自爾而粲然矣；以律小大之稱，則親疎貴賤男女之理，皆於此乎形見，幽隱者自爾而昭灼矣。不有以著萬物之理乎？夫樂之爲用，能奮德
translation_en:
…how could there be no accomplished effects to speak of? The virtue of the human heart lies hidden in stillness, with no radiance initially visible. Music alone can stir it into activity. When the singing achieves harmony [?], the gentleness and compliance accumulated within cannot conceal the flowering of their excellence. When the dancers’ ranks interweave, the beauty and goodness rooted in the heart cannot restrain their impulse toward free expression. The deeper the feeling, the more manifest its patterned expression; its radiance will surely go still further and shine ever more brightly. Why is this? Virtue resides within music; thus, when music arises, its radiance is stirred into manifestation. This is the inevitable outcome.

The vital energies of the four seasons circulate in Heaven, and it might seem difficult to ensure that all are harmonious. Music alone can set them in motion. Expressed through sound and movement, it strengthens harmony with harmony, so that the benevolent activity of spring and summer does not dissipate. Applied to bells and chime stones, it assists compliance with compliance, so that the righteous stillness of autumn and winter does not become closed off. The deeper its influence, the more wondrous its transforming power; the preservation and integration of the true workings of life will surely follow their proper course without deviation. Why is this? Music arises from Heaven; thus, when music is performed, harmony is activated, through workings that admit of no interruption.

As for the principles of the myriad things, they are so intricate that they cannot be fully recorded, yet music can make them manifest. The fullness of its sound and vital energy communicates with the ordered relationships of things; thus, the accord of its rhythms finds natural expression in its forms and movements. By aligning the sequence of endings and beginnings, it presents images of the principles governing ruler, ministers, people, affairs, and things: what was undifferentiated thereby becomes distinctly clear. By regulating the due proportions of small and great, it gives visible expression to the principles governing close and distant kin, noble and lowly, male and female: what was hidden thereby becomes brilliantly manifest. Does it not thus make manifest the principles of the myriad things? Now, music in its operation can stir virtue into activity…

title: 嘉靖四十年貴州鄉試錄
嘉靖四十年貴州鄉試錄
text:
及也而不知所以爲君子者道也道非外物也
而所以統之者心也以心求道道具於吾心矣
以道循名名在是矣苟外心以求道則道爲虛
位外道以循名則名爲過情道以有本而立亦
以無本而窮不於其本之立而欲其道之行此
殆驩虞之術耳孰謂君子之道若是哉夫子告
子路脩己以安百姓爲君子夫是道也其諸盡
性以盡人之性以盡物之性與天地參者乎獨
惜乎子路之未達也請申之天之生斯人也天
===
命之理具於吾心渾然完固在天不加益在吾
心不加損所謂各具一太極者也衆人梏而小
之斯爲小人矣所謂百姓日用而不知也君子
知吾心本體之大而求以充其量不越乎敬而
已矣蓋理欲之勢彼此相乘使一念之不謹一
息之或怠則欲得以乘之而萬事萬物之本於
是乎壞焉故曰敬者德之聚也君子於不覩不
聞也則戒愼焉恐懼焉於隱微也則愼獨焉若
視聽若言動以至起居食息無往而不愼焉然
punctuated:
及也，而不知所以爲君子者道也。道非外物也，而所以統之者心也。以心求道，道具於吾心矣；以道循名，名在是矣。苟外心以求道，則道爲虛位；外道以循名，則名爲過情。道以有本而立，亦以無本而窮。不於其本之立，而欲其道之行，此殆驩虞之術耳，孰謂君子之道若是哉？夫子告子路，脩己以安百姓爲君子。夫是道也，其諸盡性以盡人之性，以盡物之性，與天地參者乎？獨惜乎子路之未達也，請申之。
天之生斯人也，天命之理具於吾心，渾然完固，在天不加益，在吾心不加損，所謂各具一太極者也。衆人梏而小之，斯爲小人矣，所謂百姓日用而不知也。君子知吾心本體之大，而求以充其量，不越乎敬而已矣。蓋理欲之勢，彼此相乘，使一念之不謹，一息之或怠，則欲得以乘之，而萬事萬物之本於是乎壞焉。故曰：「敬者德之聚也。」君子於不覩不聞也，則戒愼焉，恐懼焉；於隱微也，則愼獨焉。若視聽，若言動，以至起居食息，無往而不愼焉。然
translation_en:
…reaching it [?], yet not knowing that what makes one a gentleman is the Way. The Way is no external thing; what unifies it is the heart-mind. Seek the Way through the heart-mind, and the Way is fully present within our own heart-minds; follow the Way to live up to the name, and the name is justified therein. If one seeks the Way apart from the heart-mind, the Way becomes an empty position; if one pursues the name apart from the Way, the name exceeds the reality. The Way is established by having a foundation, and comes to an impasse through lacking one. To desire that the Way be practiced without establishing its foundation is surely no more than a technique for winning favor. Who would say that the gentleman’s Way is like this? The Master told Zilu that being a gentleman means cultivating oneself so as to bring peace to the common people. Is this Way not that of fully realizing one’s own nature, thereby fully realizing the natures of other people and of things, and taking one’s place alongside Heaven and Earth? It is regrettable only that Zilu had not yet understood this. Allow me to explain further.
When Heaven brings human beings into existence, the principles of Heaven’s mandate are fully present within our heart-minds, whole, complete, and secure. In Heaven they are no greater; in our heart-minds they are no less. This is what is meant by saying that each possesses a Supreme Ultimate in its entirety. Ordinary people fetter and diminish this, thus becoming petty people. This is what is meant by saying that the common people use it daily without knowing it. The gentleman knows the greatness of the original substance of his heart-mind and seeks to realize its full capacity. This requires nothing beyond reverent attentiveness. For principle and desire each seek to gain the upper hand over the other. Should a single thought be unguarded, or vigilance slacken for a single breath, desire can exploit the opening, and the foundation of all affairs and things is thereby ruined. Thus it is said: “Reverent attentiveness is where virtue gathers.” The gentleman is cautious and apprehensive concerning what he neither sees nor hears; in what is hidden and subtle, he is watchful over himself when alone. In seeing and hearing, speaking and acting, and even in rising, retiring, eating, and resting, he is never without care. Only then…

title: 嘉靖四十年貴州鄉試錄
text:
後吾心之本體不引於物不淆於人天之所以
賦於我者始克全而無害矣夫若是者不過求
吾之心脩吾之身初何與於人何與於百姓殊
不知隔於形骸者分也限於遠近者勢也夫人
之心不同而同有是理百姓之衆寡不同而同
有是心吾以是心肇於此百姓則以是心通於
彼吾以是心感之百姓亦以是心孚之若桴之
應鼓影之隨形蓋有不期然而然者何也百姓
有生之初同具是理者也特蔽於欲鑿於人其
===
本然之體所謂知能之良固在也其初本同而
人自異之君子不過因其自然之性以感發之
耳是豈日令而月申家驅而戶迫哉故易曰有
孚惠心有孚惠我德書曰王道正直會其有極
歸其有極詩曰民之秉彝好是懿德使君子於
此若曰天下之大百姓之衆而吾以一心之微
一人之身烏能通於天下而使之安乃從事刑
政之末知術之巧以爲鼓舞天下之計則寡雖
應而衆必違近雖從而遠必悖暫雖舉而久必
punctuated: 後吾心之本體不引於物，不淆於人，天之所以賦於我者始克全而無害矣。夫若是者，不過求吾之心，脩吾之身，初何與於人，何與於百姓？殊不知隔於形骸者，分也；限於遠近者，勢也。夫人之心不同，而同有是理；百姓之衆寡不同，而同有是心。吾以是心肇於此，百姓則以是心通於彼；吾以是心感之，百姓亦以是心孚之。若桴之應鼓，影之隨形，蓋有不期然而然者。何也？百姓有生之初，同具是理者也。特蔽於欲，鑿於人，其本然之體，所謂知能之良，固在也。其初本同，而人自異之，君子不過因其自然之性以感發之耳。是豈日令而月申，家驅而戶迫哉？故《易》曰：「有孚惠心，有孚惠我德。」《書》曰：「王道正直，會其有極，歸其有極。」《詩》曰：「民之秉彝，好是懿德。」使君子於此若曰：「天下之大，百姓之衆，而吾以一心之微，一人之身，烏能通於天下而使之安？」乃從事刑政之末，知術之巧，以爲鼓舞天下之計，則寡雖應而衆必違，近雖從而遠必悖，暫雖舉而久必
translation_en:
…only then will the original substance of my heart neither be drawn away by things nor confused by human influences, and what Heaven has endowed me with can at last remain whole and unharmed. Such a person does no more than seek his own heart and cultivate his own person. What has this, at first sight, to do with others, or with the common people? Yet this overlooks the fact that separation by bodily form is a matter of distinct individual allotments, and limitation by distance a matter of circumstances. People's hearts differ, yet all possess this same principle; the common people may be many or few, yet all possess this same heart. When I make a beginning here with this heart, the people respond there through this same heart. When I move them with this heart, they too respond in trust through this same heart. Like the correspondence between drumstick and drum, or a shadow following a form, this happens without being deliberately sought. Why is this? From the beginning of life, the people all possess this same principle. Though obscured by desires and impaired by human contrivance, their original substance—their innate moral knowledge and capacity—certainly remains. Originally they were alike; people themselves have made themselves different. The gentleman merely works through their natural dispositions to stir and awaken them. How could this mean issuing orders daily and repeating injunctions monthly, driving each family and coercing every household?

Thus the Book of Changes says: “There is sincerity in a beneficent heart; there is sincerity in repaying my virtue with kindness.” The Book of Documents says: “The kingly way is straight and upright. Gather toward the supreme standard; return to the supreme standard.” The Book of Odes says: “The people hold fast to their constant nature and love this admirable virtue.” Suppose the gentleman were to say at this point: “All under Heaven is so vast, and the people so numerous. With the minuteness of my single heart and the person of one man, how can I reach all under Heaven and bring them peace?” If he then occupied himself with the secondary matters of punishments and administration and with clever intellectual stratagems, taking these as his means of stirring all under Heaven into action, then, though a few might respond, the multitude would surely resist; though those nearby might obey, those far away would surely rebel; though his measures might be put into effect for a time, in the long run they would surely…

title: 嘉靖四十年貴州鄉試錄
text:
選蒭菲兼收網羅求圖緯之才葑菲靡棄
伏念臣巴州寒士數學末流一藝粗通懶
未聞乎大道幾年殫力敢自負於
明朝乃製渾儀實稽往牒本諸張平子創物眞
立法之精詳傳於顏延之入關信絕代之
奇祕上規下矩儀天地之象形左鼓右鐘
定晦明之刻數仰窺俯察表裏類於雞丸
觀象玩占運行譬乎蟻磨地足地輪地軸
崇臺有架閣之陳中關小關定關密室置
===
圓機之運氣朔具瞻咫尺乾坤不出戸庭
雖一得之微勞荷
九重之采納乃於告成之日擢以渾儀之丞念
保章之官非通儒莫授而經緯之任豈庸
才能勝臣敢不益盡方寸之長罄竭涓埃
之助勉精舊學衍洪範五行之疇圖效微
誠陳豳風七月之候伏願
聖躬天保
帝德日新上下同流極財成輔相之道陰陽順
punctuated:
選蒭菲兼收，網羅求圖緯之才，葑菲靡棄。
伏念臣巴州寒士，數學末流，一藝粗通，懶未聞乎大道；幾年殫力，敢自負於明朝。乃製渾儀，實稽往牒，本諸張平子創物，眞立法之精詳；傳於顏延之入關，信絕代之奇祕。上規下矩，儀天地之象形；左鼓右鐘，定晦明之刻數。仰窺俯察，表裏類於雞丸；觀象玩占，運行譬乎蟻磨。地足、地輪、地軸，崇臺有架閣之陳；中關、小關、定關，密室置圓機之運。氣朔具瞻，咫尺乾坤，不出戸庭。雖一得之微勞，荷九重之采納。乃於告成之日，擢以渾儀之丞。念保章之官，非通儒莫授；而經緯之任，豈庸才能勝？臣敢不益盡方寸之長，罄竭涓埃之助，勉精舊學，衍《洪範》五行之疇；圖效微誠，陳《豳風》《七月》之候。
伏願聖躬天保，帝德日新，上下同流，極財成輔相之道，陰陽順
translation_en:
… In selecting men, you take in even humble grasses and vegetables, casting your net widely for men skilled in astronomical charts and celestial patterns, discarding neither turnip nor radish.
I humbly reflect that I, your servant, am an impoverished scholar of Bazhou, a minor practitioner of the mathematical arts. I have a rough command of one skill, but through indolence [?] have yet to hear the Great Way. After several years of exhausting effort, I venture to take pride in my ability before this enlightened court. I therefore constructed an armillary sphere, carefully consulting earlier records. It was based on Zhang Pingzi’s invention, truly precise and thorough in its underlying methods; transmitted through Yan Yanzhi’s entry into the passes [?], it is indeed a marvelous secret unequaled in its age. Circular above and square below, it models the forms of Heaven and Earth. With a drum to the left and a bell to the right, it determines the numbered intervals of darkness and daylight. Observed upward and downward, its inner and outer parts resemble an egg [?]; in observing celestial forms and pondering their indications, its movement may be likened to an ant on a millstone. Its base supports, base wheel, and base axle are arranged on a framework upon a lofty terrace; its central joint, small joint, and fixed joint enable the circular mechanism to operate within an enclosed chamber. The solar terms and new moons can all be observed: Heaven and Earth lie within a few inches, without one’s leaving the courtyard. Although this was but the slight achievement of a single insight, it received Your Majesty’s gracious acceptance. On the day of its completion, I was accordingly promoted to Assistant Director in charge of the Armillary Sphere.
I reflect that the office of Astrologer should be entrusted only to a scholar of comprehensive learning; how could a mediocre talent discharge the responsibility for tracing the celestial coordinates? How dare I, your servant, fail to make still fuller use of my modest abilities and exhaust my contributions, tiny as a drop of water or a speck of dust? I shall strive to perfect my previous learning and elaborate the category of the Five Phases in the “Great Plan.” Seeking to demonstrate my humble sincerity, I shall set forth the seasonal signs described in “The Seventh Month” among the “Airs of Bin.”
I humbly wish that Heaven may protect Your sacred person and that Your imperial virtue may be renewed each day; that those above and below may move together, fulfilling to the utmost the Way of ordering and assisting the workings of Heaven and Earth; and that yin and yang may follow their proper …
